summaries.intermediate: Nelson et al. (Scientific Reports, 2024) show that Drosophila glia prune olfactory sensory neuron synaptic glomeruli after critical-period odor exposure. Experience drives neuropil infiltration and Draper/MEGF10-dependent pruning, Basket/JNK versus Puckered signaling for nuclear JNK, and Cheerio/FLNA-dependent actin remodeling required for phagocytosis.
summaries.advanced: The cascade is reported for this OSN-to-projection-neuron glomerulus system during a defined critical period; reversibility mentioned in the opening is not re-quantified in the mechanistic results summary. Catalog stage is proofreading; organism fly.

plain_language_summary: Young fruit flies trim smell-system connections to match the odors they meet. Support cells called glia move in, recognize the targets, and eat those synapses using a chain of stress and skeleton-building molecules.

ocar.opportunity: Comparing whole-nervous-system molecular identities across species can reveal how brains evolve.
ocar.challenge: Whether neuronal cell-type identities remain stable while signaling systems diverge was unknown at single-neuron-class resolution across Caenorhabditis.
ocar.action: Toker et al. (bioRxiv, 2024) generate whole-animal single-cell transcriptomes of three Caenorhabditis species spanning more than 45 million years.
ocar.resolution: Neuron-class identities are remarkably stable, with combinatorial homeodomain transcription factors among the best classifiers of homologs. Neurotransmitter-producing identities stay stable, but ionotropic and metabotropic receptors diverge so that more than half of neuron classes change receptivity. Neuropeptides and receptors diverge while wireless-network topology stays dense; novel small secreted proteins show similarly cell-type-specific, evolvable expression.
ocar.future_work: They propose these patterns as candidate principles for evolutionary novelty in neuronal circuits.

summaries.beginner: Comparing three roundworm species, the same neuron types can still be recognized after tens of millions of years. What changes most is which chemical messages those cells can hear, even when the senders stay the same.
summaries.intermediate: Toker and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2024) compare whole-animal single-cell transcriptomes across three Caenorhabditis species separated by more than 45 million years. Homologous neuron classes remain identifiable, especially via homeodomain codes. Transmitter-producing identities are stable, but receptor complements shift in more than half of classes; neuropeptidergic expression diverges while overall wireless-network density remains stable.
summaries.advanced: “More than 45 million years” and “more than half of all neuron classes” are the quantitative claims in the abstract. Receptor “capacity” is transcriptomic, not physiological. Catalog dataset DS01 C. elegans; stage graph analysis. This is a preprint.

plain_language_summary: Comparing three roundworm species, the same neuron types can still be recognized after tens of millions of years. What changes most is which chemical messages those cells can hear, even when the senders stay the same.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics needs to link mesoscale fluorescence maps with electron-microscopy ultrastructure and with functional imaging, including in aging and disease models.
ocar.challenge: Existing recombinant rabies tools did not span that range of reporters, subcellular targeting, live calcium imaging, automation, and dual EM/fluorescence in one resource set.
ocar.action: Bouin et al. (Molecular Psychiatry, 2024) report 20 new recombinant rabies vectors for multi-scale, multi-modal circuit mapping.
ocar.resolution: Variants express improved fluorescent proteins, target neuronal subcellular locations, reveal microstructural changes in aging and Alzheimer’s mouse models, enable live calcium imaging, support automated neuron measurement, and encode GFP plus ferritin for dual EM and mesoscale imaging.
ocar.future_work: The suite is intended to expand rabies-mediated labeling and circuit mapping across scales in health and disease.

summaries.beginner: A classic virus used to trace brain circuits is rebuilt in many versions that glow better, mark cell parts, report activity, or show up in both light and electron microscopes. The new kit is tested in aging and Alzheimer’s model mice.
summaries.intermediate: Bouin and colleagues (Molecular Psychiatry, 2024) introduce 20 recombinant rabies vectors for multi-scale mapping. They demonstrate improved fluorophores, subcellular targeting, detection of microstructural changes in aging and AD mouse models, live calcium imaging, automated infected-neuron measurement, and GFP–ferritin dual EM/fluorescence reporters.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not report a whole-brain EM volume. Catalog method is electron microscopy; organism mouse. Rabies cytotoxicity and tropism remain general caveats not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: A classic virus used to trace brain circuits is rebuilt in many versions that glow better, mark cell parts, report activity, or show up in both light and electron microscopes. The new kit is tested in aging and Alzheimer’s model mice.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian connectomes are spatially embedded and volumetrically constrained, so how brain volume relates to topology is a basic open question.
ocar.challenge: Prior comparative samples rarely spanned orders of magnitude in brain size with a common reconstruction method.
ocar.action: Puxeddu et al. (PLoS Biology, 2024) analyze the MaMI database: 201 animals, 103 species, 12 taxonomic orders, brain size spanning more than 4 orders of magnitude.
ocar.resolution: As volume increases, modules become more spatially compact and dense with costlier connections; node distance increasingly limits communication efficiency; smaller brains are more routing-efficient and larger brains more diffusion-efficient; modular structure constrains signaling more in larger brains.
ocar.future_work: The authors conclude that spatial embedding imposes tighter restrictions as brains grow.

summaries.beginner: Bigger mammal brains are not just scaled-up small brains. Across more than a hundred species, larger brains pack their connection neighborhoods more tightly, and distance matters more for how signals could travel.
summaries.intermediate: Puxeddu et al. (PLoS Biology, 2024) relate connectome topology to brain volume in MaMI (201 animals, 103 species, 12 orders, >4 orders of magnitude in size). Larger brains have more compact, dense, costly modules; distance weighs more on communication; routing versus diffusion efficiency trades off with size; modules constrain signaling more in larger brains.
summaries.advanced: Connectomes are from this MRI-style mammalian database, not synaptic EM. Communication “policies” are network models. Counts 201/103/12 and “more than 4 orders of magnitude” are from the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Bigger mammal brains are not just scaled-up small brains. Across more than a hundred species, larger brains pack their connection neighborhoods more tightly, and distance matters more for how signals could travel.

ocar.opportunity: Mouse models remain central to Alzheimer’s mechanism and therapy work in the United States, where AD is described as the most common neurodegenerative disease.
ocar.challenge: Overexpression transgenic models of familial mutations can distort proteinopathy; newer knock-in/knock-out and CRISPR models aim to avoid human-gene overexpression for familial and sporadic risk genes.
ocar.action: Zhong, Peng, Duarte, Wang, and Cai (Molecular Neurodegeneration, 2024) review commonly used and newly developed AD mouse models in translational labs.
ocar.resolution: They summarize presence or absence of amyloid, tau, degeneration, and cognitive phenotypes, advantages and limits, sex-specific features, and omics signatures versus human AD brains to guide model choice.
ocar.future_work: The stated hope is that molecular-signature matching will help labs pick models fit for particular research questions.

summaries.beginner: Alzheimer’s research in mice has used many genetic strains, some of which overload the brain with human proteins. This review compares older and newer mouse models so labs can pick ones that better match human disease features.
summaries.intermediate: Zhong et al. (Molecular Neurodegeneration, 2024) review AD mouse models from overexpression transgenics to KI/KO and CRISPR lines. They tabulate amyloid and tau pathology, degeneration, behavior, sex differences, and omics resemblance to human AD, discussing advantages and limitations for translational research.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a head-to-head new experiment. Catalog organism is mouse; stages empty. “Most common neurodegenerative disease in the United States” is the abstract’s epidemiological framing.

plain_language_summary: Alzheimer’s research in mice has used many genetic strains, some of which overload the brain with human proteins. This review compares older and newer mouse models so labs can pick ones that better match human disease features.

ocar.opportunity: Diffuse low-grade glioma typically strikes young, active adults; untreated, it invades widely, malignantly transforms, and kills, yet connectome-based awake surgery can delay transformation while preserving quality of life through network reconfiguration.
ocar.challenge: Patients differ enormously in tumor course and in how their brains reorganize, so a single treatment sequence is inadequate.
ocar.action: Duffau (Journal of Personalized Medicine, 2022) reviews a multistage longitudinal strategy that tries to stay one step ahead of each patient’s glioma and plasticity.
ocar.resolution: He argues for predicting growth rate, migration, mutations, seizure and cognitive risk, and spatiotemporal redistribution so that surgery and (neo)adjuvant treatments are timed before malignant transformation, using patient-specific tumoral and non-tumoral markers.
ocar.future_work: The program is prospective personalization rather than a completed trial; future work is to sharpen those predictive markers.

summaries.beginner: A slow-growing brain tumor in young adults can still turn aggressive if left alone. This article argues for planning each person’s surgeries and drugs around how their tumor and their brain networks are likely to change over years.
summaries.intermediate: Duffau (J. Pers. Med., 2022) outlines a personalized longitudinal strategy for diffuse low-grade glioma. Maximal connectome-based awake resections, repeated as needed, aim to postpone malignant transformation while networks reconfigure. Because tumor kinetics and plasticity vary, he emphasizes predicting both glioma evolution and brain adaptation to time treatments before clinical worsening.
summaries.advanced: This is a strategic review from a surgical-connectomics perspective, not a randomized outcome study. Catalog stage is infrastructure. Claims about postponing transformation summarize the author’s program rather than new trial statistics in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: A slow-growing brain tumor in young adults can still turn aggressive if left alone. This article argues for planning each person’s surgeries and drugs around how their tumor and their brain networks are likely to change over years.

ocar.opportunity: Selective network vulnerability in people at Alzheimer’s risk might separate pathological from normal aging before symptoms, enabling earlier intervention.
ocar.challenge: Isolating circuits that track a composite of age, APOE genotype, and sex, and then predicting those risk variables from connectomes, is statistically hard in modest samples.
ocar.action: Mahzarnia et al. (Cerebral Cortex, 2022) study 72 people across the lifespan, enriched for APOE4, using sparse CCA and an extension of tensor-network PCA, plus sparse regression.
ocar.resolution: CCA linked genotype-weighted risk to subgraphs involving cuneus, temporal, cingulate, and cerebellum; adding cognition highlighted pericalcarine, insula, superior temporal sulcus banks, and cerebellum. Predictive errors were 17% for genotype, 24% for family risk, and 5 years for age. Age models including cognitively impaired subjects implicated additional temporal, paracentral, amygdala, and parahippocampal regions.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the models as stepping stones toward single-subject prediction.

summaries.beginner: Brain connection patterns may show Alzheimer’s risk before memory fails. In a lifespan sample enriched for a high-risk gene, certain networks predicted gene type, family risk, and age, with extra regions appearing when impaired people were included.
summaries.intermediate: Mahzarnia et al. (Cerebral Cortex, 2022) analyze 72 participants, APOE4-enriched, with sparse CCA relating a composite AD risk factor to vulnerable subgraphs, then sparse models predicting genotype (17% error), family risk (24%), and age (5 years). Including cognitively impaired subjects in age prediction recruited additional medial temporal and related regions.
summaries.advanced: n = 72 is modest for high-dimensional connectomes; errors are reported without an external replication cohort in the abstract. Catalog stages list graph analysis; organism tags empty (human sample).

plain_language_summary: Brain connection patterns may show Alzheimer’s risk before memory fails. In a lifespan sample enriched for a high-risk gene, certain networks predicted gene type, family risk, and age, with extra regions appearing when impaired people were included.

ocar.opportunity: Thalamic neuromodulation is increasingly used for drug-resistant epilepsy because the thalamus participates in multiple epilepsy types.
ocar.challenge: Best targets, programming, and mechanisms remain incompletely known; imaging must both justify targets and reconstruct electrode placement.
ocar.action: Middlebrooks, He, Grewal, and Keller (Epilepsy Research, 2022) review neuroimaging and thalamic connectomics in epilepsy neuromodulation.
ocar.resolution: They cover structural and functional thalamic changes across epilepsy syndromes, imaging of thalamic nuclei, the case for direct surgical targeting rather than only stereotactic coordinates, and neuroimaging as a biomarker of stimulation effects and outcomes.
ocar.future_work: The review positions imaging-defined connectomics as a route to better target selection and outcome prediction.

summaries.beginner: Stimulating the thalamus can help some people whose seizures resist drugs. This review explains how brain scans of thalamic connections can guide where to place electrodes and how to judge whether stimulation is working.
summaries.intermediate: Middlebrooks et al. (Epilepsy Research, 2022) review thalamic neuroimaging in neuromodulation for epilepsy. They discuss syndrome-specific thalamic network changes, nucleus imaging, arguments for direct targeting over atlas coordinates, and imaging biomarkers of stimulation effects and outcomes.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new trial. Catalog stages and organism tags are empty. No numeric outcome rates appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Stimulating the thalamus can help some people whose seizures resist drugs. This review explains how brain scans of thalamic connections can guide where to place electrodes and how to judge whether stimulation is working.

ocar.opportunity: Olfactory dysfunction is considered a pre-cognitive biomarker of Alzheimer’s disease, and olfaction is highly conserved, so mouse AD models are widely used to study smell loss.
ocar.challenge: Early detection in mice requires well-chosen behavioral assays that actually engage relevant olfactory cortex.
ocar.action: Zhang et al. (Brain Sciences, 2022) review olfactory evaluation of AD model mice, covering traditional tests, behaviors involving olfactory cortex, and published results in AD models.
ocar.resolution: The review aims to inspire further development of olfactory detection methods in AD model mice.
ocar.future_work: Methodological development, not a new mouse strain, is the stated forward path.

summaries.beginner: Loss of smell can appear before memory problems in Alzheimer’s. This review surveys how researchers test smell in Alzheimer’s-model mice and which brain areas those tests likely use.
summaries.intermediate: Zhang et al. (Brain Sciences, 2022) review olfactory behavior testing in AD mouse models as a route to early dysfunction detection. They discuss traditional assays, tasks involving olfactory cortex, and findings across models, seeking to guide better detection methods.
summaries.advanced: As a review, it does not meta-analyze effect sizes in the abstract. Catalog organism is mouse; stages empty.

plain_language_summary: Loss of smell can appear before memory problems in Alzheimer’s. This review surveys how researchers test smell in Alzheimer’s-model mice and which brain areas those tests likely use.

ocar.opportunity: Diffuse low-grade gliomas are poorly circumscribed, with isolated tumor cells beyond MRI margins, creating an intermediate peritumoral zone where glioma cells and neural tissue interact.
ocar.challenge: Most peritumoral-zone work has focused on high-grade gliomas; DLGG-specific cellular, metabolic, and radiological features needed review to guide surgery and medical therapy.
ocar.action: Silva, Vivancos, and Duffau (Brain Sciences, 2022) review PTZ in DLGG and its oncological and functional implications for a connectome-guided attitude.
ocar.resolution: They argue that better PTZ delineation supports connectome-based supratotal resection (removing PTZ plus tumor core) to delay malignant transformation and improve seizure control, timing of (neo)adjuvant therapy based on infiltration pattern, and drugs targeting PTZ including immunotherapy and anti-epileptic strategies.
ocar.future_work: They call for further multimodal PTZ investigation to maximize long-term DLGG outcomes.

summaries.beginner: Slow gliomas extend invisibly beyond the MRI blob into a mixed zone of tumor and working brain. This paper argues that mapping that zone, and sometimes removing it when networks allow, could slow the cancer and help seizures without wrecking function.
summaries.intermediate: Silva et al. (Brain Sciences, 2022) review the peritumoral zone of diffuse low-grade gliomas. They discuss cellular, metabolic, and imaging features and argue that connectome-guided supratotal resection of PTZ plus core, plus infiltration-pattern-timed medical therapy and PTZ-targeted drugs, could improve oncological and functional outcomes.
summaries.advanced: Therapeutic claims (prolonged survival, seizure control) summarize a surgical philosophy; the abstract does not report new trial numbers. Catalog stages are empty.

plain_language_summary: Slow gliomas extend invisibly beyond the MRI blob into a mixed zone of tumor and working brain. This paper argues that mapping that zone, and sometimes removing it when networks allow, could slow the cancer and help seizures without wrecking function.

ocar.opportunity: Typical and atypical brain development across the perinatal period can be studied if large, motion-tolerant, multimodal MRI datasets with rich collateral information are shared.
ocar.challenge: Fetal and neonatal imaging on a single scanner with specialized sequences is logistically and technically demanding.
ocar.action: Edwards et al. (Frontiers in Neuroscience, 2022) describe the Developing Human Connectome Project neonatal data release.
ocar.resolution: The project collected 1228 multimodal MRI datasets from 1173 fetal and/or neonatal participants with demographic, clinical, family, neurocognitive, and genomic data. This neonatal release includes 783 infants (583 healthy term-born, plus preterm and high-risk infants) and 887 datasets, many longitudinal; fetal data are to be released separately.
ocar.future_work: The paper explains acquisition, processing, and access so the community can use the open resource.

summaries.beginner: A large public set of baby brain scans, many with extra health and genetic information, is now available. It covers healthy full-term newborns as well as premature and high-risk infants, sometimes scanned more than once.
summaries.intermediate: Edwards et al. (Front. Neurosci., 2022) release dHCP neonatal data: from a project totaling 1228 multimodal MRI datasets in 1173 participants, this drop includes 783 infants (583 healthy term-born plus preterm and high-risk) and 887 datasets, with motion-tolerant protocols on one scanner and rich collateral data. Fetal data will come separately.
summaries.advanced: Counts 1228, 1173, 783, 583, and 887 are from the abstract (the abstract repeats collateral-data phrasing). Catalog stages are acquisition and graph analysis. This is a resource paper, not a biological result.

plain_language_summary: A large public set of baby brain scans, many with extra health and genetic information, is now available. It covers healthy full-term newborns as well as premature and high-risk infants, sometimes scanned more than once.

ocar.opportunity: Microglia regulate synaptic pruning, transmission, and plasticity, and abnormal microglia–neuron interaction is implicated in autism, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer’s disease.
ocar.challenge: Iba1/Aif1 has long been a microglial marker whose function was unidentified.
ocar.action: Lituma et al. (PNAS, catalog year 2021) characterize global Aif1−/− mice.
ocar.resolution: Juvenile knockouts show reduced ATP-induced microglial motility and ramification, altered pruning-related proteins, fewer excitatory synapses and reduced synaptic drive in hippocampus, yet diminished synaptic engulfment; synapse number is already reduced in early postnatal hippocampus when formation predominates. Adult mice have persistent synaptic deficits plus impaired object recognition and social interaction.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest modifying microglial function could be therapeutic in neurodevelopmental, neuropsychiatric, and neurodegenerative disorders.

summaries.beginner: A protein long used just to stain immune-like brain cells turns out to matter for how those cells move and how synapses grow. Mice missing it have fewer excitatory connections and later trouble with memory and social behavior.
summaries.intermediate: Lituma et al. (PNAS, 2021) show that deleting microglial Iba1 (Aif1) impairs process motility and ramification, alters pruning-associated proteins, and reduces excitatory synapse number and drive in juvenile hippocampus, with reduced engulfment capacity and early postnatal synapse deficits. Adults retain synaptic deficits and show object-recognition and social-interaction impairments.
summaries.advanced: Global knockout affects Iba1 wherever it is expressed; the abstract attributes phenotypes to microglia but does not report a microglia-restricted conditional. Catalog organism tags are empty; journal listed as PNAS with a bioRxiv DOI. Therapeutic suggestion is speculative.

plain_language_summary: A protein long used just to stain immune-like brain cells turns out to matter for how those cells move and how synapses grow. Mice missing it have fewer excitatory connections and later trouble with memory and social behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Multimodal MRI can relate large-scale gradients in microstructure and connectivity, but open datasets that include multiple connectome flavors and gradients at several parcellations are scarce.
ocar.challenge: Researchers need raw and derived human data spanning T1, quantitative T1, diffusion, and resting-state fMRI plus ready-made connectomes.
ocar.action: Royer et al. (Scientific Data / catalog journal bioRxiv, 2021) share MICA-MICs: 50 healthy adults (23 women; 29.54 ± 5.62 years) scanned at 3 T.
ocar.resolution: Release includes anonymized raw data and brain-wide connectomes from resting-state fMRI, diffusion tractography, microstructure covariance, and geodesic cortical distance, plus gradients at multiple parcellation scales, on CONP and OSF.
ocar.future_work: The dataset is intended to facilitate studies of coupling among microstructure, connectivity, and function.

summaries.beginner: Fifty healthy adults were scanned with several MRI types that describe tissue, wiring, and activity. The team shares both the raw scans and ready-made connection maps at several spatial scales.
summaries.intermediate: Royer et al. (2021) present MICA-MICs, a 3 T multimodal MRI resource from 50 healthy adults (23 women; 29.54 ± 5.62 years): high-resolution T1, myelin-sensitive quantitative T1, diffusion, and resting-state fMRI, plus derived functional, tractography, microstructure-covariance, and geodesic-distance connectomes and gradients across parcellations.
summaries.advanced: Sample is 50 healthy adults, not a clinical cohort. Catalog journal field says bioRxiv while the DOI is s41597 (Scientific Data); use the catalog year 2021. Catalog stages are infrastructure and graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: Fifty healthy adults were scanned with several MRI types that describe tissue, wiring, and activity. The team shares both the raw scans and ready-made connection maps at several spatial scales.

ocar.opportunity: Deep brain stimulation can reduce obsessive-compulsive symptoms, but clinical use is limited by uncertainty about the best target and mechanism.
ocar.challenge: Local effects at the electrode may be less important than changes in broader networks, and studies appear to conflict on pathways.
ocar.action: Baldermann et al. (Biological Psychiatry, 2021) critically review connectomic DBS studies in OCD, combining connectivity analyses with neuromodulation results.
ocar.resolution: They work toward a unified network that, when modulated cortically or subcortically, alleviates obsessions and compulsions, seeking to merge common and diverse pathways.
ocar.future_work: The proposed unified network is a synthesis to be tested in prospective targeting.

summaries.beginner: Brain-stimulation treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder may work by changing a network, not just the spot touching the electrode. This review tries to draw one wiring picture that explains why different targets can help.
summaries.intermediate: Baldermann and colleagues (Biological Psychiatry, 2021) review connectomic deep brain stimulation for OCD. They argue that distributed networks rather than single sites explain benefit, scrutinize conflicting pathway findings, and propose a unified effective network for cortical or subcortical modulation.
summaries.advanced: This is a critical review/synthesis, not a new DBS trial. Catalog stages empty. No response-rate numbers appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Brain-stimulation treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder may work by changing a network, not just the spot touching the electrode. This review tries to draw one wiring picture that explains why different targets can help.

ocar.opportunity: Undergraduate neuroscience majors now face connectomics and other “-omics” that use graph theory and large datasets, while graduation math is still often one year of calculus plus a statistics course focused on normal-theory tests.
ocar.challenge: Students lack computational tools for big neural datasets, and credit hours are already packed with biology and premed requirements; some faculty feel their own quantitative skills have atrophied.
ocar.action: Hoy (Neuroscience Letters, 2021) comments that neuroscience undergraduates should take data-science courses common in social sciences and that quantitative training must be taught in neuroscience context.
ocar.resolution: He notes that systems neuroscience is done by interdisciplinary teams and that whole-brain connectomes in fly, zebrafish, and mouse appear regularly. He suggests workshops, journal clubs, independent studies, and web videos as stopgaps so students and instructors learn together.
ocar.future_work: The commentary urges curricular change rather than presenting a tested course sequence.

summaries.beginner: Brain-wiring research now produces huge datasets, but many college neuroscience programs still teach little data science. This commentary says students need more quantitative skills, taught with real neuroscience examples, even if that starts as a workshop.
summaries.intermediate: Hoy (Neuroscience Letters, 2021) argues that calculus-plus-classical-statistics requirements leave neuroscience majors unprepared for connectomics-scale data. He recommends data-science coursework and context-rich quantitative teaching, and he proposes faculty–student workshops and online materials as interim remedies.
summaries.advanced: This is opinion/commentary, not an education trial. Catalog lists graph analysis and mouse, which do not fully reflect the piece’s curricular focus. No outcome metrics are given.

plain_language_summary: Brain-wiring research now produces huge datasets, but many college neuroscience programs still teach little data science. This commentary says students need more quantitative skills, taught with real neuroscience examples, even if that starts as a workshop.

ocar.opportunity: The NIH BRAIN Initiative aims to understand circuit function through new technologies, which only matter if they are validated and disseminated.
ocar.challenge: Making BRAIN-funded tools usable and accessible requires coordinated strategies among innovators, funders, and partners.
ocar.action: Litvina et al. (Journal of Neuroscience, 2019) describe early dissemination strategies and spotlight investigator teams presenting at the SfN 2019 mini-symposium.
ocar.resolution: Highlighted resources span EM- and fluorescence-based connectomics, immunolabeling, and tools for recording and analyzing functional connectivity, from subcellular composition to brain-wide networks.
ocar.future_work: The article seeks a dialogue on turning products into mature, integrated, adaptable research systems.

summaries.beginner: A US brain-research initiative funds new tools, but tools only help if other labs can use them. This article points to several shared technologies for mapping and recording circuits and asks how to spread them.
summaries.intermediate: Litvina et al. (J. Neurosci., 2019) outline BRAIN Initiative dissemination goals and showcase teams providing community tools: integrated EM and fluorescence connectomics, improved immunolabeling, and functional-connectivity recording/analysis resources across scales.
summaries.advanced: This is a community/minisymposium piece, not a single methods validation. Catalog dimension is graph-analysis with empty stages. No performance numbers are given.

plain_language_summary: A US brain-research initiative funds new tools, but tools only help if other labs can use them. This article points to several shared technologies for mapping and recording circuits and asks how to spread them.

ocar.opportunity: A 3D atlas of human axonal pathways would serve education, science, and clinical work, including stimulation and surgery.
ocar.challenge: Diffusion tractography is indirect and limited; classical neuroanatomy knowledge is hard to merge with MRI in a shared workspace.
ocar.action: Petersen et al. (Neuron, 2019) build a holographic interface populated with human histology and structural MRI and convene expert neuroanatomists to define cortical, basal-ganglia, and cerebellar axonal trajectories.
ocar.resolution: The effort translates decades of anatomical knowledge into a human axonal pathway atlas applicable to educational, scientific, or clinical investigations.
ocar.future_work: The atlas is positioned for use wherever tractography needs an anatomical prior or teaching aid.

summaries.beginner: MRI tract pictures of human pathways are indirect and can be wrong. This project uses holograms so anatomy experts can draw major axon routes onto real human brain images and histology.
summaries.intermediate: Petersen et al. (Neuron, 2019) introduce a holographic platform combining human histological and structural MRI data. Expert neuroanatomists interactively defined axonal trajectories of cortical, basal ganglia, and cerebellar systems, producing an atlas meant to complement diffusion tractography.
summaries.advanced: The atlas is expert-defined, not automatically derived from a new whole-brain tracer study. Catalog stages are infrastructure and graph analysis. The abstract does not report quantitative agreement metrics among experts.

plain_language_summary: MRI tract pictures of human pathways are indirect and can be wrong. This project uses holograms so anatomy experts can draw major axon routes onto real human brain images and histology.

ocar.opportunity: Birds show mammal-like cognition without a six-layered cortex, and they possess a hippocampal formation homologous to mammals, making comparative hippocampal connectomics informative for evolution and mind.
ocar.challenge: Whether avian HF shows anterior–posterior specializations in connectivity and adult neurogenesis, analogous to mammalian long-axis differences, was unclear.
ocar.action: Herold et al. (Cortex, 2019) apply 3D polarized light imaging to pigeon HF and measure adult neurogenesis across subdivisions and caudal regions.
ocar.resolution: Pigeon HF shows regional specialization of connectivity along the anterior–posterior axis and different adult-neurogenesis levels by subdivision and caudal region, indicating functional specialization along that axis despite species-specific morphology.
ocar.future_work: The data feed the debate on hippocampal evolution by coupling conserved connectivity and neurogenesis traits with species-specific form.

summaries.beginner: Birds remember and navigate without a mammal-style layered cortex. In pigeons, the hippocampus-like region still changes in its wiring and in new-cell birth from front to back, as mammal hippocampi do in their own way.
summaries.intermediate: Herold et al. (Cortex, 2019) use 3D polarized light imaging to show that pigeon hippocampal formation has anterior–posterior specializations in connectivity, plus subdivision- and caudal-dependent adult neurogenesis. They interpret this as functional long-axis specialization with conserved hippocampal traits despite distinct morphology.
summaries.advanced: Comparisons to mammals are qualitative in the abstract. Catalog stages and organism tags are empty. 3D-PLI reports fiber orientation architecture, not synapses.

plain_language_summary: Birds remember and navigate without a mammal-style layered cortex. In pigeons, the hippocampus-like region still changes in its wiring and in new-cell birth from front to back, as mammal hippocampi do in their own way.

ocar.opportunity: Comparative connectomics within primates can reveal human specializations and those of other species relative to shared architecture.
ocar.challenge: Long-range connections improve communication but cost energy and space; how connectivity scales with brain size and which links are human-specific remained to be synthesized across methods.
ocar.action: Rilling and van den Heuvel (Brain, Behavior and Evolution, 2018) review primate comparative connectomics using white-matter volume, histology, tracing, dMRI, and functional connectivity.
ocar.resolution: Larger primate brains appear less well connected globally, yet humans have more connections than expected for cortical neuron number, possibly concentrated in prefrontal cortex. Human-specific structural and resting-state links involve language, imitation, tool use, and empathy, atop widespread overlap with nonhuman primates.
ocar.future_work: They urge expanding species coverage via postmortem dMRI, careful homologies, better tractography, and linking connectivity to behavior within and across species.

summaries.beginner: Comparing monkey, ape, and human brain networks suggests bigger primate brains are, overall, less densely linked, while humans may have extra connections in areas used for language and tools. Better scans of more species are needed to test that picture.
summaries.intermediate: Rilling and van den Heuvel (Brain Behav. Evol., 2018) review primate connectomics. They report that larger primate brains are less well connected, that humans exceed expectation for neuron number (possibly in prefrontal cortex), and that human-specific structural and functional connections involve language, imitation, tool use, and empathy. They discuss methods and the need for more species and better homology/tractography.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; quantitative “more than expected” is not given a number in the abstract. Catalog stages are proofreading and graph analysis; organism other (primates). Tractography false positives/negatives are explicitly flagged as future-method needs.

plain_language_summary: Comparing monkey, ape, and human brain networks suggests bigger primate brains are, overall, less densely linked, while humans may have extra connections in areas used for language and tools. Better scans of more species are needed to test that picture.

ocar.opportunity: Autism is often discussed as long-range underconnectivity plus short-range overconnectivity, which should leave a signature in the corpus callosum, the major interhemispheric axon bundle.
ocar.challenge: Whether axon number, diameter, and segment-specific diversity differ across five functionally distinct callosal segments in autistic versus neurotypical people needed electron-microscopic morphometry.
ocar.action: Wegiel et al. (Acta Neuropathologica Communications, 2018) compare nine neurotypical and nine autistic subjects across five CC segments.
ocar.resolution: Average axon diameter and cross-sectional area are reduced in autism; small axons (<0.651 μm) increase in percentage while large axons (>1.051 μm) decrease. Total small-diameter axons fall 43% on average in segments I and III; medium- and large-diameter axons fall in all five segments by averages of 49% and 72%. Patterns suggest failed axon guidance and failed control of axon structure, which could slow and thin signal transmission and distort segment specialization.
ocar.future_work: The authors interpret axon-number and axon-size deficits as components of connectome-integrity distortion that may contribute to the autism phenotype.

summaries.beginner: The thick cable linking the two brain halves has fewer and thinner long fibers in the autistic people studied here. That change could slow messages between hemispheres and blur the usual differences among parts of that cable.
summaries.intermediate: Wegiel et al. (Acta Neuropathol. Commun., 2018) use EM morphometry on five corpus-callosum segments in nine autistic and nine neurotypical subjects. They report smaller average axon diameter and area, a shift toward small-diameter axons, 43% fewer small axons in segments I and III, and 49% and 72% average reductions of medium- and large-diameter axons in all segments, interpreting this as developmental failure of guidance and axon-structure control.
summaries.advanced: n = 9 per group is small; causality versus autism phenotype is interpretive. Diameter cutoffs 0.651 and 1.051 μm and percentages 43/49/72 are from the abstract. Catalog stage segmentation; method electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: The thick cable linking the two brain halves has fewer and thinner long fibers in the autistic people studied here. That change could slow messages between hemispheres and blur the usual differences among parts of that cable.

ocar.opportunity: From embryo to infancy, brain structure and function change rapidly and can be imaged, but adult neuroimaging concepts do not transfer directly.
ocar.challenge: Acquisition and interpretation require knowledge of fetal/neonatal structural and physiological development and of modulators such as the placenta, plus awareness of each modality’s technical and biological limits.
ocar.action: Vasung et al. (NeuroImage, 2018) review developmental milestones of transient structures and axonal connectivity, contributions of ex vivo and in vivo MRI, synaptic-circuit development, neurovascular coupling and metabolism, and functional connectivity, comparing MRI, EEG, MEG, and NIRS, and emerging placental MRI.
ocar.resolution: They summarize what imaging has taught about early development and stress that much remains, with a need for technical innovation if early interventions are to avert long-term disease.
ocar.future_work: The review frames early fetal and infant intervention as a future potential that still depends on better methods.

summaries.beginner: A baby’s brain changes fast, so adult scan methods cannot be copied blindly. This review explains how MRI and other tools watch those early changes and why the placenta and the baby’s unique biology still limit what we can see.
summaries.intermediate: Vasung et al. (NeuroImage, 2018) review structural and physiological neuroimaging of early human brain development. They cover transient structures, axonal and synaptic connectivity, neurovascular coupling, metabolism, and functional connectivity across MRI, EEG, MEG, and NIRS, plus placental MRI as a modulator, and they catalog technical and biological limitations.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new cohort. Catalog stage is graph analysis. No new quantitative developmental curves are claimed in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: A baby’s brain changes fast, so adult scan methods cannot be copied blindly. This review explains how MRI and other tools watch those early changes and why the placenta and the baby’s unique biology still limit what we can see.

ocar.opportunity: Deep brain stimulation is highly effective for movement disorders and is being tested for other indications, but outcome depends on exact electrode placement and on relating location to clinical effects.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing electrodes and stimulation volumes from clinical or high-field MRI poses many neuroimaging challenges, and the original Lead-DBS methods paper was out of date relative to community-added tools.
ocar.action: Horn et al. (catalog year 2018; NeuroImage/bioRxiv) present Lead-DBS v2: updated open-source DBS and connectome pipelines, demonstrated on a 3 T example and a 51-patient 1.5 T Parkinson cohort.
ocar.resolution: The pipeline spans co-registration, nonlinear warps, electrode reconstruction, volume-of-tissue-activated models, tractography, and structural/functional connectivity. In 51 PD patients they compare how much variance in clinical improvement different method choices explain.
ocar.future_work: The toolbox is positioned to empower future DBS imaging and connectomics studies as a multi-institutional open-source effort.

summaries.beginner: Brain-stimulation treatment only works well if the electrode sits in the right place. This open software helps doctors and researchers reconstruct that placement from MRI and estimate which brain networks the stimulation touches.
summaries.intermediate: Horn et al. (2018) describe Lead-DBS v2, an open-source pipeline for DBS imaging and connectomics. Updates include multispectral registration, connectivity analyses, brain-shift correction, MER reconstruction, and segmented-lead orientation. They illustrate methods on a high-field case and a 51-patient 1.5 T Parkinson cohort, comparing how preprocessing choices affect explained variance in clinical improvement.
summaries.advanced: The 51-patient comparison is retrospective PD; generalizability to other indications is not claimed. Catalog journal is bioRxiv; stages include alignment, segmentation, infrastructure, and graph analysis. Multiple alternative algorithms are offered rather than a single mandated default.

plain_language_summary: Brain-stimulation treatment only works well if the electrode sits in the right place. This open software helps doctors and researchers reconstruct that placement from MRI and estimate which brain networks the stimulation touches.

ocar.opportunity: Three-dimensional genome folding (TADs and loops) regulates transcription, and most schizophrenia risk variants are common and likely regulatory, so the brain’s spatial genome may structure genetic risk.
ocar.challenge: How 3D genome architecture, development, and cell type shape SZ risk, including genes far from risk loci on the linear map, was poorly understood.
ocar.action: Rajarajan et al. (Science, 2018) use Hi-C during isogenic differentiation of human iPSC neural progenitors into neurons or astrocyte-like glia, mapping cell-type-specific chromosomal contacts at SZ risk loci.
ocar.resolution: Differentiation remodels loops (pruning and de novo contacts). Neurons and NPCs host more SZ-anchored interactions than glia. Risk-locus contacts expand the gene set by 50–150% via “risk locus–connect” genes (e.g., NPC 386 genes: 146 in loci + 240 connected; neuron 385; glia 201), enriching neuronal connectivity/synaptic-plasticity regulators and chromatin proteins with evidence of coordinated transcription and protein interaction. Conformational changes at SZ sequences disproportionately occur in neurons.
ocar.future_work: The work highlights cell-type-specific 3D-genome vulnerabilities in schizophrenia risk.

summaries.beginner: DNA folds in 3D so distant switches can control genes. In lab-grown human brain cells, schizophrenia risk stretches of DNA touch extra genes especially in neurons, expanding the list of genes that may matter.
summaries.intermediate: Rajarajan et al. (Science, 2018) map chromosomal conformations as human iPSC neural progenitors become neurons or glia. SZ-associated common-variant sites participate in cell-type-specific loops that add 50–150% more genes beyond those in the loci themselves, with neuronal enrichment for connectivity and chromatin regulators and coordinated expression/proteomic interaction. 3D remodeling at risk sequences is disproportionate in neurons.
summaries.advanced: Gene counts (386/385/201 and splits) and the 50–150% expansion are from the abstract; they are Hi-C spatial proximity, not proven causation. CRISPR is mentioned as functional validation in the structured abstract. This is chromosomal “connectome,” not synaptic wiring. Catalog stage graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: DNA folds in 3D so distant switches can control genes. In lab-grown human brain cells, schizophrenia risk stretches of DNA touch extra genes especially in neurons, expanding the list of genes that may matter.

ocar.opportunity: Two-sample testing of whether two graphs share generating structure arises in neuroscience, social networks, and machine learning.
ocar.challenge: For latent-position graphs on a shared vertex set, a consistent test was needed for equal latent positions or scaled/diagonal transformations of them.
ocar.action: Tang et al. (2017) propose a test statistic from spectral decompositions of each adjacency matrix for random dot product graphs.
ocar.resolution: The procedure is valid and consistent across a broad range of alternatives. It distinguishes test–retest neural connectome scans from different subjects and distinguishes chemical versus electrical C. elegans networks even at small sample size.
ocar.future_work: They discuss relations to generalized likelihood-ratio tests.

summaries.beginner: Sometimes you need a yes/no answer: are these two networks generated the same way? A spectral test can tell apart different people’s brain scans and even the chemical versus electrical wiring maps of a worm.
summaries.intermediate: Tang et al. (2017) develop a semiparametric two-sample test for random dot product graphs using spectral embeddings of adjacency matrices. It tests equal latent positions or scaled/diagonal transforms. Applications distinguish between-subject neural connectomes in a test–retest set and chemical versus electrical C. elegans connectomes, with power even at small samples.
summaries.advanced: Catalog journal field is empty; year 2017. Validity is for the stated latent-position class. Dataset DS01 C. elegans; stage graph analysis. “Small-sample” power is claimed for the worm example without a numeric n in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Sometimes you need a yes/no answer: are these two networks generated the same way? A spectral test can tell apart different people’s brain scans and even the chemical versus electrical wiring maps of a worm.

ocar.opportunity: A Google-Earth-like map of neural structure at every scale is required to understand information flow, including in large-animal brains.
ocar.challenge: Imaging and processing then used in connectomics could not complete large-animal brains within a typical research career.
ocar.action: Hwu, Margaritondo, and Chiang (BMC Biology, 2017) present a Q&A on synchrotron x-ray tomography as an in situ multi-scale connectome-mapping approach, arguing feasible improvements in x-ray imaging could change the timeline.
ocar.resolution: They position synchrotron x-ray tomography as an exciting route to whole-brain wiring diagrams at multiple resolutions.
ocar.future_work: The piece is prospective: it discusses why to use the method rather than delivering a completed large-animal connectome.

summaries.beginner: Mapping every wire in a large brain with today’s usual methods would take longer than a career. This Q&A argues that powerful x-ray imaging at a synchrotron could map whole brains at several zoom levels in place.
summaries.intermediate: Hwu et al. (BMC Biology, 2017) argue in Q&A form that synchrotron x-ray tomography can map whole-brain wiring in situ at multiple scales, whereas then-current connectomic imaging could not finish large-animal brains in a career. They contend feasible x-ray improvements would change that outlook.
summaries.advanced: This is advocacy/explainer, not a methods benchmark with resolution and throughput numbers in the abstract. Catalog method is X-ray microscopy; stage graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: Mapping every wire in a large brain with today’s usual methods would take longer than a career. This Q&A argues that powerful x-ray imaging at a synchrotron could map whole brains at several zoom levels in place.

ocar.opportunity: Imaging cells and microvasculature in the living brain is crucial for neurobiology, but opening bone is invasive.
ocar.challenge: Intact skull scatters light, blocking synaptic-resolution two-photon imaging of cortex.
ocar.action: Zhao et al. (Light: Science & Applications, 2017) introduce a skull optical clearing window using agents (including collagenase, EDTA disodium, and glycerol) on bare mouse skull to soften bone and match refractive index.
ocar.resolution: Combined with two-photon microscopy, they repeatedly imaged neurons, microglia, and microvasculature; they studied dendritic-spine plasticity in critical periods and visualized dendrites and microglia after laser ablation. A water-immersion lens was used in vivo.
ocar.future_work: They emphasize easy handling and safety as reasons the method should see neuroscience use.

summaries.beginner: Seeing living mouse brain cells usually means removing or thinning skull. Here chemicals make the intact skull clearer so a two-photon microscope can watch neurons, immune cells, and tiny vessels, even spines.
summaries.intermediate: Zhao et al. (Light Sci. Appl., 2017) create a skull optical clearing window for synaptic-resolution cortical imaging in living mice. Clearing agents applied to bare skull enable repeated two-photon imaging of neurons, microglia, and microvasculature, plus spine-plasticity and laser-ablation experiments.
summaries.advanced: Hair and skin are removed; “non-invasive” in the secondary blurb is relative to craniotomy, not to any surgery. Catalog method is two-photon; stage acquisition; organism mouse. Safety is asserted without a toxicology table in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Seeing living mouse brain cells usually means removing or thinning skull. Here chemicals make the intact skull clearer so a two-photon microscope can watch neurons, immune cells, and tiny vessels, even spines.

ocar.opportunity: Brainhack events produce many small, open tools and standards that can accelerate neuroimaging if they are documented together.
ocar.challenge: Individual hackathon outputs are otherwise scattered and hard to cite or discover.
ocar.action: Bellec, Margulies, and many coauthors (GigaScience, 2016) publish the 2015 Brainhack Proceedings as a table of contents of short pieces.
ocar.resolution: Entries include Brainspell interface work, NiData, BIDS in C-PAC, AFNI centrality implementations, LORIS anonymization, Nipype HCP pipelines, DueCredit, NIDM API, DIPY tissue classification, and other open-science utilities.
ocar.future_work: The proceedings function as a citable snapshot of community tooling rather than a single scientific result.

summaries.beginner: A 2015 brainstorming meeting for brain-imaging software produced many small open tools. This proceedings collection lists them so others can find and use the projects.
summaries.intermediate: The 2015 Brainhack Proceedings (GigaScience, 2016) compile short reports on open neuroimaging software and standards—BIDS, Nipype HCP pipelines, NIDM, DIPY, citation tooling, data sharing, and more—rather than one hypothesis-driven study.
summaries.advanced: This is a multi-abstract proceedings, so pedagogical “resolution” is the existence of the collection, not a unified finding. Catalog stages are infrastructure and graph analysis. Do not treat any single listed tool as validated by this wrapper paper.

plain_language_summary: A 2015 brainstorming meeting for brain-imaging software produced many small open tools. This proceedings collection lists them so others can find and use the projects.

ocar.opportunity: Learning and memory involve synaptic-strength change, but experiments also show structural plasticity: synapse elimination/regeneration, spine turnover, and axon/dendrite remodeling.
ocar.challenge: A likely function of that structural change—raising the chance that Hebbian cell assemblies can be stored in sparse wiring—needed a quantitative notion of “effectual connectivity.”
ocar.action: Knoblauch and Sommer (Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 2016) define effectual connectivity as the fraction of synaptically linked pairs within a memory assembly, relate it to storage capacity and to effective connectivity in imaging/connectomics, and apply a memory model to a cortical macrocolumn.
ocar.resolution: They give improved estimates of how many assemblies a realistically connected macrocolumn can store, derive a simplified structural-plasticity model for large-scale simulation, and link ongoing adult structural plasticity to behavioral spacing effects in learning.
ocar.future_work: The simplified model is intended for large-scale simulation of memory phenomena.

summaries.beginner: Memories may live in groups of cells that need to be linked, but cortex is only sparsely wired. Growing and shrinking synapses can raise the odds that the right cells become connected, which this theory ties to how much can be stored and to spaced learning.
summaries.intermediate: Knoblauch and Sommer (Front. Neuroanat., 2016) argue structural plasticity increases effectual connectivity—the fraction of connected pairs inside a Hebbian assembly—thereby raising capacity of sparse networks. They relate the measure to information storage and to imaging “effective connectivity,” estimate assembly numbers in a cortical macrocolumn with realistic connectivity, and connect adult structural plasticity to the spacing effect.
summaries.advanced: Macrocolumn capacity figures are model estimates; the abstract does not quote the numeric capacity. Catalog stages are infrastructure and modeling. Effectual connectivity is a theoretical construct, not an EM measurement here.

plain_language_summary: Memories may live in groups of cells that need to be linked, but cortex is only sparsely wired. Growing and shrinking synapses can raise the odds that the right cells become connected, which this theory ties to how much can be stored and to spaced learning.

ocar.opportunity: If the brain is a complex system, damaging one area should have widespread consequences; the amygdala has distributed, well-defined cortical connectivity, making it a test case.
ocar.challenge: Linking a focal inactivation to remote functional-connectivity changes required a structural account, not only local effects.
ocar.action: Grayson et al. (Neuron, 2016) pharmacogenetically inactivate the rhesus monkey amygdala and measure global resting-state fMRI organization, then simulate disconnection using a graph of experimentally established structural connectivity.
ocar.resolution: Inactivation disrupted amygdalocortical communication and distributed corticocortical coupling across systems. Simulated communication capacity via mono- and polysynaptic paths largely accounted for endogenous correlations and many nonlocal changes after inactivation.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest this strategy for linking focal neuropathology to remote neurophysiological changes.

summaries.beginner: Turning off the amygdala in monkeys changed resting activity far across the brain, not only next door. A map of known anatomical paths predicted many of those distant changes.
summaries.intermediate: Grayson et al. (Neuron, 2016) inactivate the rhesus amygdala pharmacogenetically and show disrupted amygdalocortical and distributed corticocortical resting-state coupling. Graph analysis of established structural connectivity, aggregating mono- and polysynaptic communication capacity, largely accounted for baseline correlations and many nonlocal inactivation effects.
summaries.advanced: Accounting is “largely,” not complete. Catalog organism is other (rhesus); stages graph analysis and modeling. Resting-state coupling is not the same as task-evoked function.

plain_language_summary: Turning off the amygdala in monkeys changed resting activity far across the brain, not only next door. A map of known anatomical paths predicted many of those distant changes.

ocar.opportunity: Locomotion shapes mouse V1 sensory responses and is often explained by a disinhibitory motif in which Vip interneurons inhibit Sst cells, thereby releasing pyramids.
ocar.challenge: Whether that motif actually operates across stimulus sizes during locomotion was untested at the level of simultaneous cell-type responses.
ocar.action: Dipoppa et al. (bioRxiv, 2016) measure locomotion effects on Pyr, Vip, Sst, and Pvalb neurons in mouse V1 layer 2/3 with two-photon imaging.
ocar.resolution: With large stimuli, locomotion increased Sst responses without suppressing Vip; with small stimuli, locomotion increased Vip without suppressing Sst—inconsistent with a simple disinhibitory model. A circuit model reproduced each type’s activity from the others only if locomotion increased feedforward synaptic weights while modulating recurrent weights.
ocar.future_work: They conclude locomotion alters cortical function by changing effective synaptic connectivity, not only via disinhibition.

summaries.beginner: A mouse’s running changes how visual cortex responds, but not by the simple “release the brakes” circuit many expected. The data fit a picture where running retunes connection strengths among cell types.
summaries.intermediate: Dipoppa et al. (bioRxiv, 2016) image mouse V1 L2/3 Pyr, Vip, Sst, and Pvalb cells during locomotion. Large stimuli: locomotion raises Sst without suppressing Vip; small stimuli: raises Vip without suppressing Sst. Models match the data only if locomotion scales feedforward weights and modulates recurrent weights, arguing against a locomotion effect mediated only by Vip–Sst disinhibition.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2016 preprint in the catalog. Conclusions depend on the cell-type identification and stimulus-size manipulation. Catalog method two-photon; organism mouse; dimension cell-types.

plain_language_summary: A mouse’s running changes how visual cortex responds, but not by the simple “release the brakes” circuit many expected. The data fit a picture where running retunes connection strengths among cell types.

ocar.opportunity: The Human Connectome Project and related studies need a public archive that can house multimodal MRI/MEG, behavior, and demographics and deliver data at high speed.
ocar.challenge: Open sharing must balance public imaging data with restricted sensitive behavioral fields and guide users to the right subset.
ocar.action: Hodge et al. (NeuroImage, 2015) describe ConnectomeDB as the WU-Minn HCP archive and dissemination platform, also intended for the Connectome Coordination Facility.
ocar.resolution: It holds structural, task, resting-state, and diffusion MRI plus resting and task MEG, at unprocessed, minimally preprocessed, and analysis levels. Public data require data-use terms; sensitive behavior is more restricted. Delivery uses a web UI plus Aspera, hard-drive shipment, and Amazon S3.
ocar.future_work: The database is designed to expand with additional connectome-style studies.

summaries.beginner: A large public library stores human brain scans and related behavior from the Human Connectome Project. Anyone who accepts the rules can download imaging data; some sensitive behavior scores need extra approval.
summaries.intermediate: Hodge et al. (NeuroImage, 2015) present ConnectomeDB, the public-facing WU-Minn HCP database for MRI and MEG plus behavior. It serves unprocessed through analysis derivatives, with tiered access and high-speed transfer (Aspera, drives, S3), and is intended as a home for further connectome-style projects.
summaries.advanced: This is an infrastructure paper, not a biological result. Catalog stages are infrastructure and graph analysis. Performance of Aspera versus other transfer methods is not quantified in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: A large public library stores human brain scans and related behavior from the Human Connectome Project. Anyone who accepts the rules can download imaging data; some sensitive behavior scores need extra approval.

ocar.opportunity: Major depressive disorder affects multiple large-scale functional networks, prompting many resting-state connectivity studies.
ocar.challenge: Findings appear heterogeneous across seed-based and ICA papers, so a synthesizing model within existing network-dysfunction hypotheses was needed.
ocar.action: Mulders et al. (Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews, 2015) review those studies and propose a model of MDD network changes.
ocar.resolution: Despite differences, consistent patterns include increased connectivity within the anterior default-mode network, increased salience–anterior DMN connectivity, altered anterior–posterior DMN connectivity, and decreased posterior DMN–central executive connectivity—matching a view of depression as a network-based disorder.
ocar.future_work: The model is offered to organize future rs-fMRI work in MDD rather than as a closed mechanistic proof.

summaries.beginner: Depression involves changes in how large brain networks talk at rest, not only in one spot. A review finds a few repeated patterns, especially around the mind-wandering network and its links to attention and control networks.
summaries.intermediate: Mulders et al. (Neurosci. Biobehav. Rev., 2015) review seed-based and ICA resting-state studies in MDD. They highlight four relatively consistent findings involving anterior DMN, salience coupling, anterior–posterior DMN, and posterior DMN–central executive hypoconnectivity, and they embed these in network-dysfunction hypotheses of depression.
summaries.advanced: “Consistent” is a qualitative synthesis; the abstract acknowledges inter-study differences. Catalog stages empty; dimension review. No effect sizes are given.

plain_language_summary: Depression involves changes in how large brain networks talk at rest, not only in one spot. A review finds a few repeated patterns, especially around the mind-wandering network and its links to attention and control networks.

ocar.opportunity: Graph matching—aligning two graphs to minimize edge disagreements—matters in combinatorics, computer vision, and connectomics, but it is computationally hard.
ocar.challenge: Many heuristics relax the discrete permutation problem to a continuous one; few have theoretical performance guarantees, and convex versus indefinite relaxations may behave very differently.
ocar.action: Lyzinski et al. (IEEE TPAMI, 2014/2015) prove that an indefinite relaxation, solved exactly, almost always finds the optimal permutation, whereas a common convex relaxation almost always fails.
ocar.resolution: Theory suggests initializing the indefinite algorithm with the convex optimum; experiments on benchmarks and real data corroborate that amalgamating the two approaches works well.
ocar.future_work: The combined strategy is recommended for practical matching, including connectomic graphs.

summaries.beginner: Matching two networks by shuffling their labels is extremely hard. The authors prove that one popular “make it continuous” shortcut almost never finds the true matching, while another usually does, and that using both in sequence works in practice.
summaries.intermediate: Lyzinski et al. (IEEE TPAMI, 2015) analyze relaxations of graph matching. An indefinite relaxation almost always recovers the optimal permutation when solved exactly; a common convex relaxation almost always does not. Initializing the indefinite method with the convex solution yields strong benchmark and real-data performance.
summaries.advanced: “Almost always” is a theoretical statement under the paper’s random-graph conditions, not a guarantee on every connectome. Catalog stage is graph analysis; no organism/dataset tags. Catalog year is 2014.

plain_language_summary: Matching two networks by shuffling their labels is extremely hard. The authors prove that one popular “make it continuous” shortcut almost never finds the true matching, while another usually does, and that using both in sequence works in practice.

ocar.opportunity: A static localizationist view of the adult brain cannot explain widespread functional recovery after damage.
ocar.challenge: How much adult circuits can reorganize, and what limits that plasticity, needed evidence from patients undergoing repeated mapping.
ocar.action: Duffau (Cortex, 2014) reviews serial mappings in adults who had awake surgery for diffuse gliomas infiltrating eloquent structures: intraoperative cortical and subcortical stimulation, peri-operative neuropsychology and functional imaging, and remapping at reoperation for recurrence.
ocar.resolution: Massive resections of “critical” regions can avoid permanent sequelae via circuit reorganization; repeated surgeries show remapping over time. However, white-matter connectivity is a main limit on plasticity, explaining poor recovery after extensive subcortical damage.
ocar.future_work: Connectomics thus both enables and constrains a dynamic model of adult CNS plasticity.

summaries.beginner: Adult brains can reroute function around a slow tumor, even in areas once called untouchable, if the long-distance cables are spared. Repeat surgeries show that map changing over years, but cutting those cables still causes lasting loss.
summaries.intermediate: Duffau (Cortex, 2014) uses serial awake glioma surgery to argue for a dynamic, network view of adult brain processing. Intraoperative stimulation supports distributed language models; pre/post imaging and testing show large “eloquent” resections without permanent deficits; reoperations reveal remapping. White-matter connectomics is identified as the principal limit on this plasticity.
summaries.advanced: Evidence is from a surgical series/review, not a randomized trial. Catalog stages empty; dimension connectomics. “Huge plastic potential” is bounded explicitly by subcortical damage.

plain_language_summary: Adult brains can reroute function around a slow tumor, even in areas once called untouchable, if the long-distance cables are spared. Repeat surgeries show that map changing over years, but cutting those cables still causes lasting loss.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding computations requires dense measurements of activity and of wiring; zebrafish are cheap, transparent, genetically tractable, and have small brains at larval and adult stages.
ocar.challenge: Exhaustive activity imaging and EM wiring diagrams are more feasible when brains are small; motivations and methods for such dense reconstructions needed a focused review.
ocar.action: Friedrich, Genoud, and Wanner (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2013) review methods and motivations for dense reconstructions of neuronal activity and connectivity, emphasizing zebrafish advantages, with examples from olfactory-bulb computations.
ocar.resolution: Small brain size enables optical activity mapping and large-scale EM wiring reconstruction, which they argue is important and probably essential for mechanistic insight into higher functions and dysfunctions.
ocar.future_work: The olfactory bulb is presented as a working example of combining structure and function in this model.

summaries.beginner: A fish with a tiny, see-through brain makes it realistic to watch many cells fire and, later, to map how they are wired. This review explains why zebrafish are well suited to that double measurement, using the smell center as an example.
summaries.intermediate: Friedrich et al. (Front. Neural Circuits, 2013) argue that zebrafish enable exhaustive activity and connectivity measurements because of small brain size plus genetic and optical access. They review dense reconstruction methods and illustrate computational studies in the olfactory bulb, positioning such data as likely essential for mechanistic circuit insight.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/perspective, not a new EM volume. Catalog dataset DS15 zebrafish; method electron microscopy; stage graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: A fish with a tiny, see-through brain makes it realistic to watch many cells fire and, later, to map how they are wired. This review explains why zebrafish are well suited to that double measurement, using the smell center as an example.

ocar.opportunity: Graph-theoretic analyses of human connectomes need visualization, but toolboxes for drawing those networks were still lacking given methodological complexity.
ocar.challenge: Researchers needed an easy GUI to combine brain surfaces, nodes, and edges with controllable appearance and multiple views.
ocar.action: Xia, Wang, and He (PLoS ONE, 2013) introduce BrainNet Viewer, a MATLAB GUI that draws connectomes as ball-and-stick models.
ocar.resolution: Users load connectome files, adjust colors, sizes, and layouts, render surface/nodes/edges in sequence and in multiple views, interact for details, and export images or videos. The software is free on NITRC.
ocar.future_work: The tool is intended to make network visualization flexible and quick for human connectomics studies.

summaries.beginner: Drawing a human brain network as balls and sticks used to take custom code. This free MATLAB program lets researchers load connection files, adjust the picture, and export figures or movies.
summaries.intermediate: Xia et al. (PLoS ONE, 2013) present BrainNet Viewer, a MATLAB GUI for graph-based human-connectome visualization. It supports combinations of surface, nodes, and edges, extensive display settings, multi-view rendering, interaction, and export to common image formats or video, distributed via NITRC.
summaries.advanced: This is a software paper; the abstract does not include a user study. Catalog stage is graph analysis. MATLAB dependence may limit accessibility.

plain_language_summary: Drawing a human brain network as balls and sticks used to take custom code. This free MATLAB program lets researchers load connection files, adjust the picture, and export figures or movies.

ocar.opportunity: Whether adult neurogenesis causally helps recover cognition after stroke was not properly tested.
ocar.challenge: Selectively removing neuroprogenitor cells without changing infarct size or other cell genesis is required to isolate that contribution.
ocar.action: Sun et al. (Journal of Neuroscience, 2013) use nestin-δ-HSV-TK-EGFP mice with ganciclovir (200 mg/kg/d) for 4 weeks before experimental stroke, ablating baseline and stroke-induced type 1 and type 2 NPCs.
ocar.resolution: GCV duration-dependently eliminated NPCs without attenuating peri-infarct astroglia or oligodendrogenesis, infarct size, or reperfusion. Transgenic GCV mice showed impaired Barnes-maze spatial learning/memory versus saline or wild-type GCV controls, without a significant motor difference despite SVZ NPC ablation. Retrograde PRV614 from dentate gyrus labeled fewer entorhinal neurons, suggesting reduced DG–EC synaptic connectivity.
ocar.future_work: NPC ablation thus impedes poststroke cognitive recovery and may reduce perforant-path connectivity.

summaries.beginner: After a stroke, the brain grows some new nerve cells. When those precursor cells are removed in mice, memory recovery suffers even though the stroke size is unchanged, and a memory pathway looks less well connected.
summaries.intermediate: Sun et al. (J. Neurosci., 2013) conditionally ablate nestin-lineage NPCs in adult mice with GCV (200 mg/kg/d) before stroke. Ablation spares peri-infarct astroglia/oligodendrocytes, infarct size, and reperfusion, but impairs Barnes-maze spatial memory without significant motor change. Fewer PRV614-labeled entorhinal neurons after DG injection suggest reduced perforant-path connectivity.
summaries.advanced: Cognitive impairment is in transgenic+GCV versus controls; motor is not significantly different. Reduced PRV labeling is an indirect connectivity measure. Catalog stages and organism tags are empty though this is mouse stroke work. Dose 200 mg/kg/d is in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: After a stroke, the brain grows some new nerve cells. When those precursor cells are removed in mice, memory recovery suffers even though the stroke size is unchanged, and a memory pathway looks less well connected.

ocar.opportunity: Epilepsy is ultimately a disease of aberrant connections among neurons and groups of neurons, even though much recent work has focused on channels and transmitters.
ocar.challenge: Mechanisms of seizure onset and termination in humans remain unknown despite detailed clinical description and many animal models with diverse mechanisms; a bridge from microscale models to human systems is needed.
ocar.action: Engel et al. (Current Opinion in Neurology, 2013) review connectomic approaches—dMRI, fMRI, EEG at whole-brain scale; optogenetics, tracers, electrophysiology, and calcium imaging at local circuits.
ocar.resolution: These methods are already revealing network disturbances underlying epileptic abnormalities; understanding development of epilepsy and seizures will require delineating aberrant whole-brain functional and structural connections.
ocar.future_work: The authors state that connectomics now provides approaches to accomplish that systems-level delineation.

summaries.beginner: Epilepsy is a problem of how brain cells and regions connect, not only of single-cell chemistry. New wiring and activity maps at whole-brain and local-circuit scales are starting to show the networks that seizures use.
summaries.intermediate: Engel et al. (Curr. Opin. Neurol., 2013) argue that epilepsy research must move to systems-level connectivity. They review MRI, fMRI, and EEG connectomics plus local-circuit tools, note rapidly growing evidence of network disturbances, and conclude that delineating whole-brain aberrant connections is required to explain epileptogenesis and seizure generation.
summaries.advanced: This is a current-opinion review, not a new dataset. Catalog stage is graph analysis. No specific quantitative network biomarker is claimed in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Epilepsy is a problem of how brain cells and regions connect, not only of single-cell chemistry. New wiring and activity maps at whole-brain and local-circuit scales are starting to show the networks that seizures use.

ocar.opportunity: The Human Connectome Project required high-throughput collection, sharing, automated processing, mining, and visualization with consistent quality.
ocar.challenge: Maintaining data consistency over time, measuring head motion, and providing modality-specific quality scores, plus database and visualization integration, are non-trivial informatics problems.
ocar.action: Marcus et al. (NeuroImage, 2013) describe HCP quality-control procedures, XNAT-customized database services for internal operations and open sharing, and Connectome Workbench visualization increasingly tied to those services.
ocar.resolution: They report the then-current state of these tools and their application in the ongoing HCP study.
ocar.future_work: The informatics suite is meant to scale with the continuing HCP acquisition.

summaries.beginner: A huge human brain-scanning project needs automatic checks that data are good, a database people can query, and software to look at the results. This paper describes those behind-the-scenes systems for the Human Connectome Project.
summaries.intermediate: Marcus et al. (NeuroImage, 2013) present HCP informatics: quality-control methods for longitudinal consistency, head motion, and modality-specific scores; XNAT-based database services for operations and open access; and Connectome Workbench visualization integrated with those services, as used in the ongoing study.
summaries.advanced: This is an infrastructure snapshot from 2013, not a scientific finding about brain organization. Catalog stage is infrastructure. No numeric QC thresholds appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: A huge human brain-scanning project needs automatic checks that data are good, a database people can query, and software to look at the results. This paper describes those behind-the-scenes systems for the Human Connectome Project.

ocar.opportunity: A whole-brain mouse connectivity atlas for C57Bl/6J, built with double coinjections of anterograde plus retrograde tracers, can reveal reciprocal connections and interaction stations at network level.
ocar.challenge: Olfactory-bulb regional connectivity needed a public, atlas-registered, multi-fluorescent resource.
ocar.action: Hintiryan et al. (Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 2012) introduce the first open Mouse Connectome Project olfactory resource: systematic double coinjections into main olfactory bulb regions, viewable in iConnectome with atlas levels and cytoarchitectural background.
ocar.resolution: Eighteen MOB cases (~72 pathways; 36 efferent/36 afferent) are available. Analysis revealed a novel topographically arranged MOB projection roadmap, different connectivity with anterior versus posterior piriform cortex, and novel aspects of established cortical olfactory projections. AOB, AON, and other olfactory cortical injections are promised gradually.
ocar.future_work: The iConnectome platform is the ongoing public access route as more cases are added.

summaries.beginner: A public atlas shows where mouse smell-bulb regions send and receive fibers, using paired tracers that mark both directions at once. The maps reveal an orderly projection plan and different links to front versus back smell cortex.
summaries.intermediate: Hintiryan et al. (Front. Neuroanat., 2012) release UCLA Mouse Connectome Project olfactory data: double anterograde/retrograde coinjections in main olfactory bulb, with 18 MOB cases (~72 pathways) in the iConnectome viewer. They report a topographic MOB projection roadmap, distinct anterior versus posterior piriform connectivity, and some novel features of known olfactory cortical projections.
