summaries.advanced: Eighteen cases / ~72 pathways are the abstract’s counts. Catalog stages are proofreading and graph analysis; organism mouse. Completeness of “novel” projections depends on comparison with prior literature, not re-documented here.

plain_language_summary: A public atlas shows where mouse smell-bulb regions send and receive fibers, using paired tracers that mark both directions at once. The maps reveal an orderly projection plan and different links to front versus back smell cortex.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic connectivity shapes neural responses, represents sensory statistics, coordinates distributed processing, and stores structural traces of the past; that importance naturally suggests network and graph theory.
ocar.challenge: Neuroimaging needed an intellectual account of how network science, already productive in other fields, was entering neuroscience.
ocar.action: Sporns (NeuroImage, 2012) offers a personal perspective on the confluence of networks and neuroimaging, charting origins of major themes from simple graphs to the connectome.
ocar.resolution: He reviews how network approaches were beginning to contribute across neuroscience as of this 20th-anniversary-style NeuroImage piece.
ocar.future_work: The essay points forward to broader adoption of connectome thinking rather than a single empirical result.

summaries.beginner: Thinking of the brain as a network, not a list of parts, changed how imaging studies are done. This essay traces how that idea grew from simple graphs to whole-brain connection maps.
summaries.intermediate: Sporns (NeuroImage, 2012) gives a personal perspective on networks in neuroimaging. He argues connectivity is fundamental for function, representation, coordination, and memory of the past, and he charts how graph-theoretic connectomics entered many neuroscience areas.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a methods paper. Catalog stages are infrastructure and graph analysis. No new dataset is introduced.

plain_language_summary: Thinking of the brain as a network, not a list of parts, changed how imaging studies are done. This essay traces how that idea grew from simple graphs to whole-brain connection maps.

ocar.opportunity: Brains dynamically switch among tasks and sleep states; epileptic brains add paroxysmal seizures, yet onset and termination mechanisms in humans are unknown despite detailed description and many experimental models with diverse mechanisms.
ocar.challenge: There is a gap between microscale experimental mechanisms and human epilepsies; simplified computational models need to be scaled to the large networks in which seizures appear; connectomics maps those networks.
ocar.action: Richardson (Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry, 2012) reviews large-scale brain models of epilepsy at the meeting point of dynamics and connectomics.
ocar.resolution: He argues the stage is set to couple dynamics with connectomics to reveal abnormal network dynamics that allow seizures.
ocar.future_work: The program is to test computer-derived dynamic mechanisms back in biological systems at whole-brain scale.

summaries.beginner: Seizures emerge in large brain networks, not only in a dish. This article says computer models of brain dynamics should be built on maps of real connections so we can see how those networks flip into a seizure.
summaries.intermediate: Richardson (JNNP, 2012) reviews the need to bridge microscale epilepsy models and human seizures using computational dynamics on large-scale connectomes. He argues that coupling dynamics with connectomics can reveal network conditions that permit seizure onset and termination.
summaries.advanced: This is a conceptual review. Catalog stage is modeling; dimension neuroai. No new patient series is reported.

plain_language_summary: Seizures emerge in large brain networks, not only in a dish. This article says computer models of brain dynamics should be built on maps of real connections so we can see how those networks flip into a seizure.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome-based simulations must span local circuits (~10^5 neurons, up to 10^9 synapses on ordinary clusters) up to brain-scale networks that are orders of magnitude larger; the first job is checking data consistency and constraining unknown parameters.
ocar.challenge: On machines such as Blue Gene/P, memory per core becomes the bottleneck as models enter meso- and macroscale, and prior brain-scale simulations were not described reproducibly or released.
ocar.action: Kunkel et al. (Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 2012) build a linear model of NEST memory consumption versus network size and core count, identify dominant components, and implement sparse local data structures.
ocar.resolution: The adaptations enable scaling to the order of 10,000 processors and beyond.
ocar.future_work: They argue the memory analysis approach should help any software handling complex connectomes on similar architectures.

summaries.beginner: Simulating a whole-brain-sized network used to run out of computer memory before time ran out. This paper shows how to predict that memory use and how to store sparse wiring so the simulator can run on tens of thousands of processors.
summaries.intermediate: Kunkel et al. (Front. Neuroinform., 2012) show that memory on each compute node, not only compute, limits brain-scale NEST simulations. A linear model of memory versus size and core count identifies bottlenecks; exploiting sparseness of local network representations scales NEST to on the order of 10,000 processors and beyond.
summaries.advanced: “On the order of 10,000 processors” is the scaling claim; exact neuron/synapse counts at that scale are not in the abstract. Catalog stage is modeling; dimension neuroai. The paper addresses NEST specifically though lessons are generalized.

plain_language_summary: Simulating a whole-brain-sized network used to run out of computer memory before time ran out. This paper shows how to predict that memory use and how to store sparse wiring so the simulator can run on tens of thousands of processors.

ocar.opportunity: fMRI and diffusion MRI studies all produce connectivity matrices that are compact, graph-analyzable, and still carry individual differences such as age, IQ, or disease.
ocar.challenge: There was no common web repository to share those matrices and run graph metrics without local tooling.
ocar.action: Brown et al. (Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 2012) introduce the UCLA Multimodal Connectivity Database for sharing and analyzing CMs.
ocar.resolution: Users share matrices, compute graph metrics on-site, visualize reports, or download raw CMs. At publication, over 2000 individual CMs spanned fMRI and dwMRI and disorders including Alzheimer’s, autism, and ADHD. A 60-subject (ages 26–45) demo finds low correspondence between functional and structural global and nodal graph measures.
ocar.future_work: The repository is intended to enable larger-scale meta-analyses across modality, age, and disease.

summaries.beginner: Many labs summarize brain scans as a table of connection strengths. This website lets them upload those tables, compute network scores in the browser, and compare across studies and diseases.
summaries.intermediate: Brown et al. (Front. Neuroinform., 2012) present the UCLA Multimodal Connectivity Database for sharing connectivity matrices and computing graph theory online. More than 2000 CMs had been contributed across modalities and disorders. In 60 adults, functional versus structural graph measures showed low correspondence, illustrating cross-modal comparison.
summaries.advanced: “Over 2000” matrices and n = 60 for the demo are from the abstract. Low functional–structural correspondence is for that example, not a universal law. Catalog stages are infrastructure and graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: Many labs summarize brain scans as a table of connection strengths. This website lets them upload those tables, compute network scores in the browser, and compare across studies and diseases.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding neocortical microcircuits requires synaptic connectivity between identified cell classes, including how layer 1 inhibitory neurons talk to layer 2/3 pyramids.
ocar.challenge: L1 is diverse; without a classification tied to connection specificity, superficial inhibitory control of pyramids remains underspecified.
ocar.action: Wozny and Williams (Cerebral Cortex, 2011) record 266 visually identified rat somatosensory L1 neurons (P24–36), classify them by Petilla physiology and anatomy, confirm four groups with unsupervised clustering, and pair them with L2/3 pyramids (n = 384 connection tests).
ocar.resolution: Four groups emerge: neurogliaform (72), classical-accommodating (137), fast-spiking (23), and burst-spiking (34). All groups except neurogliaform received monosynaptic excitation from L2/3 pyramids (33 connections; 68 NGFC pairs tested with none). Neurogliaform cells strongly inhibited L2/3 pyramids (12 of 27 pairs).
ocar.future_work: The data reveal high specificity of excitatory and inhibitory connections in superficial neocortex.

summaries.beginner: The top layer of rat cortex contains several kinds of inhibitory cells that do not all wire the same way. One type strongly shuts down the pyramids below but does not get a direct kick back from them; other types do.
summaries.intermediate: Wozny and Williams (Cerebral Cortex, 2011) classify 266 rat somatosensory L1 neurons into neurogliaform, classical-accommodating, fast-spiking, and burst-spiking groups, supported by anatomy and clustering. In 384 paired recordings with L2/3 pyramids, all classes except neurogliaform received monosynaptic pyramidal excitation, whereas neurogliaform cells inhibited pyramids in 12 of 27 tested pairs.
summaries.advanced: Counts 266, 72/137/23/34, 384, 33, 68, and 12/27 are from the abstract. Catalog organism is other (rat). Classification uses Petilla scheme plus clustering; molecular identity is not claimed.

plain_language_summary: The top layer of rat cortex contains several kinds of inhibitory cells that do not all wire the same way. One type strongly shuts down the pyramids below but does not get a direct kick back from them; other types do.

ocar.opportunity: Digital tracing of axons and dendrites from light microscopy enables quantitative morphology and computational modeling, and automation promises speed, accuracy, and reproducibility needed for high-throughput screening and connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Despite algorithm advances, manual tracing remained the dominant choice for digitizing neuronal morphology.
ocar.action: Donohue and Ascoli (Brain Research Reviews, 2010) overview issues in automated reconstruction, available techniques, and realistic future perspectives.
ocar.resolution: They summarize why automation is still hard and what would be required for it to take over as imaging throughput rises.
ocar.future_work: They expect automated reconstruction to become central as cellular imaging and microscopy accelerate, but they caution that the field had not yet displaced manual tracing.

summaries.beginner: Turning microscope pictures of a neuron into a digital tree is still mostly done by hand. This review explains the computer methods that aim to do it automatically and why they had not yet taken over.
summaries.intermediate: Donohue and Ascoli (Brain Res. Rev., 2010) review automated reconstruction of neuronal morphology from optical microscopy. They cover tracing issues, available algorithms, and prospects for high-throughput screening and connectomics, while noting that manual tracing still dominated.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2010 overview; later community challenges are outside the abstract. Catalog stages include acquisition, proofreading, and modeling. No numeric accuracy leaderboard is given.

plain_language_summary: Turning microscope pictures of a neuron into a digital tree is still mostly done by hand. This review explains the computer methods that aim to do it automatically and why they had not yet taken over.

ocar.opportunity: Formation and elimination of dendritic spines can change synaptic connectivity without major arbor remodeling, contributing to structural plasticity.
ocar.challenge: How much connectivity-pattern diversity spines can provide depends on how completely nearby axons already occupy possible synaptic slots on a dendrite.
ocar.action: Stepanyants, Hof, and Chklovskii (Neuron, 2002) define the filling fraction as the ratio of synapses on a dendrite to axons passing within a spine length of that dendrite, and they calculate it from geometry and anatomical data.
ocar.resolution: The filling fraction is 0.26 in mouse neocortex and 0.22–0.34 in rat hippocampus. In macaque visual cortex it increases by a factor of 1.6–1.8 from V1 to V2, V4, and 7a. Because the fraction is much smaller than 1, spine remodeling can contribute substantially to structural plasticity.
ocar.future_work: Regional differences in filling fraction, including the V1-to-higher-area increase in macaque, suggest different capacities for spine-based rewiring along the visual hierarchy.

summaries.beginner: A nerve cell’s branches are not fully booked by nearby wires; only about a quarter of possible contacts are filled in mouse cortex. That leftover room means growing or shrinking spines can rewire a lot without moving the main branches.
summaries.intermediate: Stepanyants et al. (Neuron, 2002) introduce the filling fraction—synapses on a dendrite divided by axons within a spine length—and estimate 0.26 in mouse neocortex and 0.22–0.34 in rat hippocampus, with a 1.6–1.8-fold increase from macaque V1 to V2/V4/7a. Values much less than 1 imply that spine turnover can generate many connectivity patterns without arbor remodeling.
summaries.advanced: Estimates combine geometry with anatomical data; they are not from a complete EM connectome. Catalog organism is mouse though rat and macaque numbers are also reported. Filling fraction is an upper-bound style argument for plasticity capacity, not a measured turnover rate.

plain_language_summary: A nerve cell’s branches are not fully booked by nearby wires; only about a quarter of possible contacts are filled in mouse cortex. That leftover room means growing or shrinking spines can rewire a lot without moving the main branches.
